title: Clear Play Space Before You Put the Headset On
body:
A clear play space is the empty floor area you will move in while wearing a headset, free of furniture edges, cables, toys, pets, and other people. Most falls and collisions in home virtual reality happen not because the virtual world is dangerous, but because the real room was never cleared. Setting the space first turns an invisible hazard into a visible, checked routine.

How to do it: Walk the whole area on foot before starting; Move chairs, rugs that slide, and loose cables out of the area; Mark the boundary the headset shows you and stay inside it; Put pets in another room and tell other people you are about to move blindfolded by the headset; Recheck the space whenever you change rooms or someone else has used the room.

What to check: Stand in the centre, stretch your arms out, and confirm you cannot reach anything hard. If the headset warns that you are near the boundary, step back to the centre before continuing, rather than leaning past the warning to finish a task.

When to stop or get help: Stop and re-clear the space if anything enters it, if you trip, or if you feel unsure where you are. A session that restarts safely is better than one that finishes with an injury.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.

area_m, area_n = 3, 3
clear = ['furniture', 'cables', 'pets', 'people']
removed = ['furniture', 'cables', 'pets', 'people']
print('play area:', area_m * area_n, 'square metres')
print('hazards cleared:', len(removed), 'of', len(clear))
print('ready:', removed == clear)

hazards cleared: 4 of 4
ready: True

title: Take Breaks and Stop at the First Sign of Discomfort
body:
Breaks in virtual reality are planned pauses in which you remove the headset, look at something distant, drink water, and let your balance settle. Discomfort in virtual reality often starts mildly, as warmth, eye tiredness, or a slight queasy feeling, and grows if you push through it. Stopping early is the skill: the headset will still be there after a rest, and your body recovers faster from a short pause than from a long spell of sickness.

How to do it: Decide your break interval before you start; Remove the headset fully at each break, not just lift it; Look away from screens, sit down, and drink water; Note how you feel on a simple scale from fine to queasy; End the session for the day if discomfort returns quickly after a break.

What to check: After a break, stand still for a few seconds and check your balance before walking. If the room still seems to move, or your stomach still feels unsettled, stay seated and end the session.

When to stop or get help: Stop at once if you feel dizzy, nauseous, sweaty, or disoriented. Do not drive, climb, or use machinery until you feel fully steady again.

title: Motion Sickness: Start Slow and Build Up Gradually
body:
Motion sickness in virtual reality comes from a mismatch: your eyes report movement while your body reports stillness. Smooth artificial movement, turning, and height changes are the strongest triggers, especially for new users. Starting with still scenes, short sessions, and teleport-style movement lets your tolerance build over days, rather than forcing one long session that ends in sickness and puts you off the technology.

How to do it: Begin with seated, still scenes and no artificial movement; Use teleport movement instead of smooth gliding where the app offers it; Turn on comfort settings such as a narrowed view during movement; Keep first sessions short and increase length only on days you felt fine; Keep a fan or cool air on your face if it helps you.

What to check: Rate your comfort after each session. If a particular movement type made you queasy, avoid it for the next session and try a gentler setting instead of repeating the same trigger at full strength.

When to stop or get help: End the session if queasiness, headache, or sweating appears. Rest until fully settled, and do not try to cure sickness by continuing in the hope you will get used to it in the same session.

title: Children and Vulnerable Users: Supervise and Follow Age Guidance
body:
Children and vulnerable users need extra care in virtual reality because their eyes, balance, and sense of what is real are still developing, and because they may not report discomfort until it is strong. The device maker's age guidance, the content rating, and an adult in the room are three separate safeguards, and none of them replaces the others. Supervision means watching the person, not just the screen.

How to do it: Read the device maker's age guidance before a child uses a headset; Choose content rated for the child's age and check it yourself first; Stay in the room and watch for tiredness, rubbing eyes, or unsteadiness; Keep sessions short and insist on breaks; Keep the headset fitted and the volume at a comfortable level.

What to check: Ask the child how they feel before, during, and after the session, in plain words. If they cannot describe what happened in the virtual scene, or seem confused about where they are, end the session and talk it through.

When to stop or get help: Stop at once if a child reports headache, dizziness, nausea, eye pain, or distress, or if they seem upset by something they saw. Do not let a child use a headset alone to calm down after a frightening experience.

title: AR Street Awareness: Never Walk Blind
body:
Augmented reality overlays digital images on the real world, which makes it easy to watch the overlay and stop watching the street. The danger is ordinary and serious: kerbs, traffic, cyclists, stairs, and other pedestrians do not pause while you read an overlay. Safe augmented reality use keeps the real world first: the overlay is a glance, not a view you walk inside.

How to do it: Stop walking before you read a long overlay or type anything; Use audio directions instead of staring at an overlay while moving; Keep one ear open to traffic where it is safe to do so; Never follow an overlay route across a road, cycle lane, or car park without looking; Take the glasses or phone down at crossings, stairs, and busy junctions.

What to check: Before crossing any road, put the device away and look both ways yourself. An overlay that says it is safe is not a substitute for your own eyes, and a route line painted over a road does not stop traffic.

When to stop or get help: Stop using the overlay at once if you feel distracted, if you have missed a kerb or a person, or if you are in traffic. Step to a safe place, then look at the device.

title: Photosensitive Seizures: Respect Flashing Content Warnings
body:
Some people are sensitive to flashing lights and rapid patterns, which can trigger seizures. Virtual and augmented content can flash faster and fill more of the visual field than a television, because the screen sits close to the eyes and surrounds them. Warnings exist for a reason, and the safest response to a warning is to skip the content or watch a non-flashing version, not to test your own tolerance.

How to do it: Read content warnings before starting a new experience; Skip or avoid content flagged for flashing lights if you or anyone in your household is photosensitive; Lower brightness and take breaks during high-contrast scenes; Sit with the room lights on if that reduces contrast; Tell others in the room about the warning so they can help you stop.

What to check: If you notice flicker, strobing, or fast alternating patterns, look away and remove the headset at once. Note the title and scene so you can avoid it and warn others.

When to stop or get help: Seek medical help promptly if you experience jerking, loss of awareness, confusion, or unusual sensations after flashing content, and do not return to flashing content until you have medical advice.

title: Eye Strain and Vision Comfort: Fit the Headset to Your Eyes
body:
Eye strain in virtual reality often comes from a poor fit rather than from the virtual world itself: lenses set too far apart or too close, a blurry image, or a headset that slips as you move. Your eyes work hardest when the image is slightly out of focus, because they keep trying to correct it. A few minutes spent fitting the headset, checking sharpness, and setting text size saves an hour of headache.

How to do it: Adjust the lens spacing to match your eyes until the image is sharp in both eyes; Set the headset so it sits level and does not press on your brow or cheeks; Increase text size where the app allows it; Check that the image stays sharp when you turn your head; Wear your usual glasses or contact lenses if you need them, with a spacer if the maker provides one.

What to check: Read a line of text in the headset and then look at a distant real object. If either stays blurry, refit before continuing. Blurry vision that persists after fitting, or pain in one eye, is a reason to stop and, if it persists, to seek eye care.

When to stop or get help: Stop if you get eye pain, double vision, or a headache that does not ease after a break and a refit. Do not share a headset fit between people with very different vision without refitting it.

title: Physical Safety: Cables, Furniture, Pets, and Other People
body:
Physical safety in virtual reality is about the room, not the software. Cables trip, coffee tables bruise shins, pets walk underfoot, and another person entering the room can collide with someone who cannot see them. A wired headset adds a trip and snag hazard of its own. The fix is a room routine that is boring on purpose: same clear space, same cable route, same warning to others, every time.

How to do it: Route cables behind you and away from walkways, or use a wireless headset where you can; Keep the play space clear and the boundary turned on; Warn others before you start and agree a word they can say to pause you; Keep drinks and hot objects out of the play space; Pause whenever someone enters the space, rather than waving them away blindly.

What to check: Do a slow turn with arms out before starting, and confirm the boundary matches the real room. If the headset tracking drifts and the boundary no longer matches the furniture, stop and reset the boundary.

When to stop or get help: Stop at once after any collision, trip, or fall, even if you feel fine. Check yourself and the room, and do not restart until the hazard that caused it is removed.

title: Privacy in Shared Virtual Spaces: What You Reveal
body:
Shared virtual spaces record more than words: voice, movement, gaze direction, room layout, and the names on your profile can all be captured, stored, or overheard. An avatar does not make you anonymous if your voice, username, or room details identify you. Privacy in virtual reality is therefore a habit of choosing, before you enter a shared space, what you are willing to reveal and to whom.

How to do it: Review microphone, camera, and tracking permissions before entering a shared space; Use a username that does not reveal your real name, school, or workplace; Keep your play-space camera view clear of personal documents and other people; Check who can hear you and who can join your session; Read the platform's data and recording rules before a public event.

What to check: After a session, check what was recorded or saved, and delete recordings you did not intend to keep. If a session was recorded without your knowledge, report it through the platform's tools and keep a note of when it happened.

When to stop or get help: Leave a space at once if someone is recording you against your wishes, asking for personal details, or following your avatar after you asked them to stop. Blocking and reporting are safety tools, not rudeness.

title: Social Safety: Blocking, Muting, and Reporting Harassment
body:
Harassment in virtual reality can feel more immediate than harassment in text, because an avatar can stand close, shout, gesture, and follow you. You are not obliged to endure it to prove toughness, and you are not obliged to debate someone who is harassing you. The platform tools exist to end the interaction fast: mute stops the sound, block stops the person, and a personal-space setting keeps avatars at a distance.

How to do it: Learn mute, block, and personal-space controls before your first public session; Turn on a personal-space boundary if the platform offers one; Mute at the first sign of harassment, without arguing; Block the account and leave the space if it continues; Report with the time, place, and username, and keep a note for yourself.

What to check: After blocking, check that the person can no longer approach or message you. If they return under a new name with the same behaviour, report that too and tell a moderator or trusted person.

When to stop or get help: Leave and seek help at once if harassment includes threats, sexual content aimed at you, or attempts to get personal information or images. Tell a trusted adult or the platform's safety team, and keep any evidence the platform allows you to keep.

title: Never Use Immersive Displays While Driving or Operating Machinery
body:
An immersive display that covers your eyes or fills your attention has no safe place in a moving vehicle or at operating machinery. Augmented overlays do not make driving safer by adding information: they add a second thing to watch while the road still needs your full attention. The same applies to cycling, using power tools, cooking over heat, and supervising children near water or roads. If the task can hurt someone when your attention lapses, the headset stays off.

What to check: If you catch yourself reaching for a headset while a task is in progress, stop the task safely first, then decide. The urge to check is the warning, not a reason to continue.

When to stop or get help: Stop the vehicle or machine safely at once if you realise you have been using an immersive display while operating it. Do not try to finish the journey or the cut first.

The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. title: A Shared-Space Safety Plan for Households
body:
A household safety plan turns separate good habits into one agreement: who may use the headset, where, for how long, and what happens when someone feels unwell or another person needs the room. Without a plan, each session renegotiates the same arguments, and the person wearing the headset is the last to know the room has changed. With a plan, everyone knows the boundary, the break rule, and the stop word.

How to do it: Agree the play space, the boundary, and the times headsets may be used; Agree a stop word anyone in the room can use; Write down break rules and maximum session lengths for each person; Agree who supervises children and who checks the fit; Review the plan after any fall, fright, or argument about headset use.

What to check: Test the plan in a short session: does the stop word actually pause the session, does everyone know the boundary, and does the headset user hear a visitor entering? If any answer is no, fix that part before longer sessions.

When to stop or get help: Suspend headset use in the household until the plan is fixed if a fall, a fright, or a privacy incident happens and the plan did not prevent it. A plan that failed silently is worse than no plan, because it gave false confidence.

title: Comfort Settings Audit: Seated Mode, Movement, and View
body:
A comfort settings audit is a systematic pass through the settings that decide how sick, strained, or startled you feel: seated or standing mode, teleport or smooth movement, snap or smooth turning, field-of-view narrowing during movement, and brightness. Most new users never open this menu, so they suffer the default settings and blame themselves. Auditing the settings before a new app turns comfort from luck into a choice.

How to do it: Set seated mode if you will sit, and standing mode only in a clear space; Choose teleport movement and snap turning for your first sessions in a new app; Turn on view narrowing during movement if offered; Set brightness and text size for comfort, not for maximum spectacle; Save a comfort profile per person where the device allows it.

What to check: Try each setting for a few minutes in a calm scene and note your comfort score. Keep the combination with the best score, and change one setting at a time when you experiment, so you know which change helped.

When to stop or get help: Reset to your known comfort profile and end the session if a new app ignores your settings or makes you ill despite them. Report the problem to the app maker with your settings noted.

title: After an Incident: Falls, Collisions, and Distress
body:
An incident in virtual reality needs the same calm response as an incident anywhere else: stop, check the person, check the room, and only then worry about the device or the game. The headset itself can delay help, because the wearer cannot see who is helping and helpers cannot see the wearer's face. Removing the headset, sitting down, and speaking plainly are the first steps, before any discussion of what went wrong.

How to do it: Remove the headset and sit or lie down; Check for pain, bleeding, dizziness, or confusion; Ask what happened in plain words and listen; Check the room for the hazard that caused the incident; Write down what happened, when, and what was changed afterwards.

What to check: If symptoms persist, worsen, or involve head injury, loss of consciousness, or confusion, seek medical help promptly and do not restart headset use that day. Keep the note of the incident for the clinician if you seek care.

When to stop or get help: Stop all headset use until the hazard is fixed and the person feels fully recovered. A second session on the same day after a head knock or a bad fright is not a test of resilience.

title: Long Sessions, Sleep, and Balance After Use
body:
Long virtual reality sessions affect more than the time they take: tired eyes, a stiff neck, disrupted sleep if sessions run late, and a brief period after use when balance and depth judgement feel slightly off. These effects are usually mild and pass, but they matter for what you do next. Planning the end of a session is part of safety, not an afterthought: finish early enough to wind down, and do not step straight from a headset into driving, cycling, or a task needing balance.

How to do it: Set a session end time before you start and keep to it; Take breaks and drink water during the session; Finish evening sessions with wind-down time away from screens; After use, sit for a minute, then stand slowly and check your balance; Avoid driving or balance-critical tasks until you feel fully steady.

What to check: Notice patterns over a week: if late sessions regularly disturb sleep, or if you regularly feel unsteady afterwards, shorten sessions and move them earlier. A pattern is information, not a personal failure.

When to stop or get help: Stop evening sessions that repeatedly disturb sleep, and seek advice if unsteadiness, eye pain, or headaches persist after you stop using the headset. Persistent symptoms deserve attention, not adaptation by pushing through.

title: Safety for Schools, Events, and Public Demonstrations
body:
Public demonstrations multiply every home risk: many different faces share one headset, fitting is rushed, supervision is thin, and the audience watches the wearer rather than the room. A public demo needs a named supervisor, a cleaning routine between users, a fitting check per person, and a clear rule that anyone may stop at any time without embarrassment. Without those, a demo that was meant to inspire becomes a queue of headaches and near-misses.

How to do it: Name one supervisor who watches users, not the screen; Clean the headset face pad between users following the maker's guidance; Fit the headset and check comfort for each person; Keep sessions short and the play space clear and guarded; Offer a non-headset way to watch, so nobody feels forced to try it.

What to check: Watch the first minute of each new user closely: if they sway, squint, or look distressed, stop and refit or end their turn. A short, comfortable demo teaches more than a long, miserable one.

When to stop or get help: Close the demo station if the play space cannot be kept clear, if cleaning cannot be done between users, or if supervision lapses. A closed station is a safety decision, not a failed event.
